children: OTTAWA--Canada's antitrust regulator has launched an investigation into the use of minimum advertised prices by the country's grocers, policies it says may be restricting competition and keeping lower prices out of reach for consumers.
Minimum advertised pricing, which can be imposed by suppliers or negotiated between suppliers and retailers, sets the lowest price at which a retailer can advertise a product.

The Competition Bureau said that in industries such as retail grocery, where a few large companies dominate the industry, these policies can make it harder for retailers such as discount grocers to offer lower prices and compete for customers.
The regulator is calling for consumers, retailers, suppliers and others to share their experience with the policies. The input will support an investigation of the sector.

"Canadians expect grocery stores to be able to advertise their best deals," Jeanne Pratt, interim commissioner of competition, said. "At a time when food affordability remains an important concern for Canadians, we want to hear about how these policies are affecting grocery prices and consumer choice."

The bureau said minimum-advertised-pricing policies can prevent retailers from advertising lower prices, even when they are prepared to offer those prices in-store. Some retailers may remove in-store discounts entirely if they can't advertise lower prices under these policies.
The country's grocery industry is concentrated in the hands of companies including Loblaw, Sobeys and Metro.

A 2023 study by the bureau found that because the big players operate thousands of stores and are well entrenched in the shopping habits of Canadians, the grocery industry is tough to break into for new players and regional independents. The regulator among the recommendations it made said provincial and territorial governments should consider introducing accessible and harmonized unit-pricing requirements. It also called for federal, provincial and territorial support to encourage the growth of independent grocers and the entry of international grocers into Canada.
